Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-16
Time: 15:00 PDT
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Jonah (Redwood SE), Aisha (Sylvan Head of ML), Tom (Sylvan Platform), Leah (Sylvan CTO)

Summary (auto):
Quick Optimize console walkthrough focused on batching and prefix/KV cache recommendations. Ran through cost model scenarios for Sylvan's 2-tier product (short chat vs longer summarization calls). Agreement to run a sandbox perf test and exchange token histograms.

Topics:
- Workload profile & SLOs
- Prefix vs session (KV) cache tradeoffs
- Batching and concurrency knobs in console
- Cost-model sensitivity to hit-rate and batch size
- Security and VPC considerations

--- Transcript body (timestamps approximate, auto-transcript, imperfect) ---
[00:00] Maya: Hi everyone, thanks for joining. quick intro, I'm Maya on the AE side, Jonah is our systems SE who will drive the technical bits. how're you all doing?
[00:10] Aisha: good, thanks. Running a bit behind but glad to be here. we've been looking at Redwood's Optimize tooling — specifically batching and caching to lower token spend.
[00:20] Jonah: Awesome, that's exactly what we planned to cover. before we dive, can you confirm the two main app patterns? short chat interactions (avg 30 tokens) and long-document summarization sessions (~1k tokens)?
[00:33] Tom: yes, that's right. about 70% of calls are short chat, 30% long sessions. peak QPS is around 120 requests/sec and we aim for p95 latency below 350ms.
[00:47] Leah: and we must keep everything inside our VPC for now — SOC2 in flight.
[00:53] Maya: perfect noted. I'll pull up the Optimize console — and the cost-model sheet — real quick. (typing)
[01:05] Jonah: high level: two levers that usually move the needle — batching (server-side continuous batching + concurrency) and prefix/KV caching (sessionization, lookahead caches). we'll show how hit-rate assumptions change cost by orders of magnitude for your mix.
[01:22] Aisha: can you remind us the difference between prefix cache and KV session cache? we've kinda mixed the terms in our doc.
[01:28] Jonah: yeah, good q. prefix cache is request-level: if you have lots of repeated prefixes (e.g. system prompts, user templates) we index by the token prefix and serve from cache. KV session cache is about keeping the model KV cache between steps in a session — think multi-turn chat where the model continues generating with a preserved KV cache. prefix is more general, KV session is higher hit-rate for long sessions.
[01:49] Tom: so for our short chats prefix is likely better, but for summarize flows KV session matters, correct?
[01:55] Jonah: exactly. prefix helps high fan-out many small requests that share starting tokens. KV helps amortize decoder cost across long sequences.
[02:03] Maya: I'll share a slide with the quick math we run in the workbook. (link pasted: https://drive.redwood/Optimize-playbook.xlsx) note: link is internal sample.
[02:13] Jonah: walking through the console, here's the Optimize tab -> 'Batch & Cache' panel, we can toggle batch size floor, max concurrency, and cache TTLs. show scenario A for Sylvan: conservative hit-rate 8% prefix, 25% KV for long sessions.
[02:28] Aisha: Those hit rates feel low to me; our UX reuses system prompts a lot. we might be 15-20% prefix.
[02:35] Jonah: cool, let's tweak it live. (typing) adjusting prefix hit to 18%, KV to 30%. console recomputes the per-token cost and shows a 22% savings vs baseline.
[02:48] Leah: nice. what assumptions for batch? you left batch at default 4.
[02:52] Jonah: default is continuous batching targeting latency SLO. the cost model uses effective batch size distribution from your token histogram if provided — otherwise a synthetic distribution. raising floor to 8 improves throughput but adds mean latency ~40ms.
[03:06] Tom: 40ms is acceptable if p95 stays under 350ms. how do you measure p95 with batching?
[03:12] Jonah: we surface latency percentile under the 'SLO sim' tab. that combines queueing latency from batching and service latency. also can simulate worst-case tail with burst traffic scenario.
[03:24] Aisha: can you show an example where cache TTL hurts? we worry side effects if a long-running session changes instructions midstream.
[03:31] Jonah: absolutely. TTL tradeoff: longer TTL increases hit-rate and reduces cost but risks staleness. we recommend short TTLs for user-intent fields and longer TTLs for stable system prompts. in the console you can set keys to 'session-scoped' — essentially KV-only — and 'prefix-global' for global reuse.
[03:49] Maya: also pragmatic: use prefix for immutable system components (instructions, brand copy) and KV session for conversation state. combine with a lookup TTL for user context fields.
[04:00] Leah: what's the overhead for managing KV across pods? ops question for Tom.
[04:06] Jonah: there's minimal network overhead — the runtime keeps KV in local GPU memory and Redis-style lookup is optional for cross-node handoff. for Dedicated/Private deployments we can provide affinity settings to keep session on the same GPU pool.
[04:20] Tom: okay, affinity needed. we can't have session hops because we don't want rewarming.
[04:25] Jonah: yep, session-affinity + sticky routing is supported; that also increases cache efficiency because you avoid KV reloads. cost model notes that affinity increases reserved capacity slightly but usually wins for high-hit scenarios.
[04:38] Aisha: can we test a hybrid: prefix mostly for short chat, KV for summarize flows, fall back to smaller model on heavy load?
[04:46] Maya: yes — routing policies can route by route or by token length. Optimize console shows per-route expected cost with fallback policies. I'll demo the routing matrix.
[04:55] Jonah: (shares screen) here's a routing rule: short_chat -> redwood-latest-small (quantized), long_summarize -> redwood-xxl with KV enabled. we simulated a 30% traffic surge and the fallback kept p95 under 500ms with a +7% cost.
[05:10] Tom: that seems reasonable. what about quantization accuracy for summarize tasks? we need quality guardrails.
[05:16] Jonah: Console integrates evals: you can attach a QA prompt set and we run metric checks on candidates. If quality drops beyond threshold, automatic rollback or steer back to higher-fidelity model.
[05:29] Aisha: this is great. show the cost-model sensitivity — like hit rate +/- 10%.
[05:33] Jonah: sure. toggling prefix hit +/-10 -> results swing from 16% savings to 26% savings. KV hit swings have bigger impact on long sessions — changing KV hit from 30% to 40% cuts long-session token spend per call dramatically.
[05:47] (small cross-talk)
[06:00] Maya: quick clarifying q — your peak is 120rps. are peaks sustained or spiky?
[06:06] Tom: spikes short, typically 30–90s. weekends heavier on summarization batch jobs.
[06:13] Jonah: solid, so lookahead prefetch might help for summarization: pre-run KV warmers as a background pipeline for known jobs. that reduces cold-starts for batch summarization and keeps tail latency consistent.
[06:26] Leah: prefetch sounds good but adds compute — how's cost compared to cold-start token spend?
[06:31] Jonah: in our workbook we put prefetch cost vs cold-start cost. typically prefetch is cheaper if you can predict sessions with >60% probability and jobs last >800 tokens. I'll send that sheet.
[06:44] Aisha: security check: since we need VPC-only, can we still use caching features?
[06:49] Jonah: yes, both prefix and KV work inside VPC/private deployments. KV persistence options can be customer-managed storage; keys can be encrypted with your KMS.
[06:58] Tom: audit logs? we need per-token auditing for SOC2.
[07:03] Maya: Console has an audit log export and token-level tracing toggles you can enable. for Private deployments logs can be shipped to your SIEM.
[07:12] Aisha: perfect.
[07:15] (fast-forward through demo: Jonah toggles settings, console updates charts)
[12:40] Jonah: jumping back to the cost model graph — this is per-100k requests baseline. note the big inflection when prefix hit passes ~12%. that's because short chats dominate calls so small prefix hits multiply across calls.
[12:55] Leah: do you model concurrency limits? we can't exceed a certain GPU footprint.
[13:00] Jonah: yes, you can set a max_concurrency per model pool, and the sim includes queuing delay. we also model burst capacity pricing if you want autoscaling above reserved.
[13:12] Aisha: about autoscale — how fast is scale up/down? and do caches survive scale-down?
[13:19] Jonah: scale up is fast (tens of seconds) for burst pools; scale down may evict caches. for persistent KV we recommend a small baseline reserved pool to hold session state; autoscale handles additional throughput.
[13:33] Tom: okay, so baseline reserved capacity is a recommended practice.
[13:37] Maya: exactly — Dedicated gives you that. in the workbook we compare reserved + burst vs pure burst pricing. in many cases reserved with optimized batching/caching is cheaper.
[13:50] Aisha: show me an end-to-end sample — from request arrival to cache hit path vs miss path.
[13:56] Jonah: sure. (walks through sequence) request arrives -> routing -> batch queue -> cache lookup (prefix index) -> if hit, short-circuit to response -> if miss, queued into GPU, decoder runs with optional KV lookup for session, response stored in prefix cache depending on policy. miss path includes additional microseconds for cache writes.
[14:25] Aisha: do you keep metrics for cache write rate? we want to ensure our keys don't grow unbounded.
[14:30] Jonah: yes we expose cache cardinality, eviction rates, hit/miss histograms. console also lets you set key digest rules and TTL auto-pruning.
[14:40] Leah: can we integrate with our existing Redis?
[14:43] Jonah: on Private deployments, yes — we can use your Redis for shared caches; for hosted we use our managed cache but can forward logs. there are tradeoffs in network latency.
[14:55] Tom: in our environment lower latency is necessary so probably local cache for KV is best.
[15:00] Maya: one more scenario: imagine you increase batch size a lot to save cost but you see increased tail. console shows a red flag and suggests reducing max concurrency or enabling streaming responses to mitigate tail.
[15:12] Aisha: streaming responses — does that change batching behavior?
[15:16] Jonah: it interacts. streaming starts sending tokens earlier which reduces perceived latency; the runtime can still batch token generation across requests, but you get smaller first-byte times. the console sim accounts for streaming benefits.
[15:31] (silence while screenshare continues)
[20:20] Maya: wrapping toward action items — recap: we'll run a sandbox test on your histogram, send the workbook and demo recording, and propose a pilot configuration (reserved baseline + burst, prefix TTLs at 6h for system prompts, KV session lifetime aligned to user session TTL).
[20:38] Tom: timeline? we'd like pilot in a two-week window.
[20:41] Jonah: we can start sandbox this week and propose pilot config by next Tue.
[20:46] Leah: confirm pricing—will you include reserved cost estimates in the sheet?
[20:50] Maya: yes, sheet will include reserved vs burst estimates and estimated monthly spend under multiple scenarios.
[20:56] Aisha: any competitor notes — we compared to CloudEndpointX which doesn't support sticky KV, and OpenServeAI has prefix cache but no integrated cost sim.
[21:08] Maya: good to record that.
[21:12] (closing)
[21:15] Maya: thanks everyone — we'll follow up with links. Jonah, anything else?
[21:19] Jonah: nothing more, looking forward to the sandbox logs.
[21:22] Leah: thanks, that was helpful.
[21:25] (call ends, small chatter)
